articles.title: Stephen Miller's internal memo unleashes Trump agencies after 'absolute control' under Wiles' reign
articles.summary: A memo under new chief of staff Stephen Miller gives Cabinet secretaries messaging control, shifting from what sources say was Susie Wiles' grip.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A memo describing the new White House hierarchy under chief of staff Stephen Miller circulated within the Trump administration this week, and details how Cabinet secretaries will now have more control over their own messaging. This is a shift from what insiders say was administration-wide communications control implemented by former chief of staff Susie Wiles during the first nearly two years of President Donald Trump's second term. "This will streamline the Cabinet, making it a more effective instrument for the President, whereas previously it was too constrained," a source familiar with the message told Fox News Digital. The memo was sent by Miller's office after he took over the role on Monday. It was titled as a memo on administrative matters and personnel changes, the source said. THE STONING OF STEPHEN MILLER, NOW RUNNING THE TRUMP WHITE HOUSE "The White House position of Cabinet Secretary will be changed to the role of Director of Cabinet Relations, focused on providing support and reinforcement of President Trump's tremendous Cabinet Secretaries," details the memo, which Fox News Digital viewed. "Each cabinet leader serves as the best leader and communicator for their individual Departments, and this new position will ensure our Cabinet is resourced and bolstered by the White House to deliver swift, critical, and lasting wins for the American people," the memo continues. Another source who is familiar with day-to-day administration operations believes the memo signals a shift in communications policy, giving different agencies the ability to control their own messaging now that Miller has become chief of staff. The source said that previously, they believe Wiles had a chokehold on nearly all the administration's communications, and that there were "a lot of prescriptive directives" from Wiles' camp. "I mean, to me, it reflects well on Miller and his team and I think it's really smart to be making these moves quite clear, to be communicating clearly and effectively, you know?" the source said, speaking of the policy shake-up described in the memo. The source added that the policy change is "unleashing the Cabinet to be the captains of their own ship." "It's more [of] a recognition that you can't possibly effectively micromanage this wide of an organization and that sometimes it might be better to trust and invest in a support system that elevates the people who are closest to the issues," the source said. TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY FACES FIRST MAJOR TEST AS WHITE HOUSE BRIEFING ROOM ENTERS NEW ERA WHITE HOUSE THREATENS POLITICO WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' IF IT DOESN'T RETRACT SUSIE WILES REPORTING A former Trump administration official had much more direct criticism of Wiles' management style. "She wants complete authority," the source said. "The control doesn't come from, 'hey, you have to do this.' The control comes from threat of duress. Like, 'if you don't do this, I'm going to destroy you in the media,'" they continued. "The thing is, she has been very clear. 'I can't control [Trump]. I can control everything else.'" The source accused Wiles of approaching Cabinet secretaries and warning them that if they said anything off script in the media, that midterm GOP election losses would be blamed on them. TRUMP CLOSING IN ON NEW PRESS SECRETARY AS ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS PUSH FOR PICK WHO COULD BREAK THE MOLD "It's absolute control," the source said. The memo also highlights some hierarchical changes within the administration, saying the director of presidential scheduling and the Office of Presidential Scheduling will report directly to Chamberlain Harris, the deputy director of outer oval operations. It also confirms previous reporting that Caleb Orr, formerly the assistant secretary of state for economic and business affairs, will become the chief of staff for policy. "The White House will run a clear and regular policy process through the Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy and the National Security Advisor, with clearly defined responsibilities and assignments and no overlapping policy portfolios," the memo says. articles.title: Pete Hegseth and others reprimanded by guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: An Arlington National Cemetery guard told the defense secretary and his companions to maintain a respectful atmosphere during a Veterans Day visit.
articles.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was reprimanded Wednesday by an Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier who asked him and his guests to maintain an atmosphere of “silence and respect.” Hegseth, his wife, Jennifer, and some of his top aides were taking pictures, talking and laughing in front of the tomb, a memorial to unidentified service members killed in battle located at Arlington National Cemetery. Hegseth had been attending a Veterans Day ceremony at which President Donald Trump laid a wreath in honor of fallen service members. The incident puts Hegseth’s name back in the headlines just one day after he narrowly dodged impeachment. Hegseth and his wife were taking pictures alongside some of his top aides when the sentinel shouted at the group: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.” Hegseth made no acknowledgment of the reprimand, looking over his shoulder and continuing to walk up a set of stairs. Asked for comment on the interaction, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth and the department “have always honored” service members’ sacrifices. “While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said in a statement. Soldiers stand watch over the tomb 24 hours a day, complete with an elaborate changing of the guard ceremony that happens at least once every hour. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a vocal critic of the Iran war who was unseated following a Trump-led effort, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth this week. The Republican-led House voted 211-204 to shelve the resolution. But Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become speaker of the House come January, has signaled Democrats will not dial back efforts to oust Hegseth. Hegseth has downplayed the efforts, calling them “political spectacle.” Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Hegseth, and he has said he would back him even if he were to be impeached.

articles.title: Longtime GOP leader faces uncertain future after Jim Jordan wins House leadership fight
articles.summary: Steve Scalise declined to commit to serving a full term in the 120th Congress after losing the House Republican minority leader race to Jim Jordan.
articles.body: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., the No. 2 Republican in the House of Representatives and the most tenured figure among the chamber's party leadership, declined to say whether he would commit to serving the full term in the upcoming 120th Congress. "There’s no decision on what’s next," Scalise said on Wednesday. "I’ve got to get through these next few weeks, and then we have a lot of decisions to make about what's life going to look like in the minority. But I sure still have a great passion for this country." JIM JORDAN THROWS HAT IN RING FOR HOUSE MINORITY LEADER AS GOP PICKS UP PIECES AFTER BLUE WAVE Scalise’s answer follows a loss to Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, in a bid to become the party’s new minority leader. His defeat now forces Scalise to decide whether he intends to retire or remain on Capitol Hill as a rank-and-file member of the minority as Democrats retake control of the House in January. For now, Scalise stressed that he remains focused on securing GOP priorities before the new year. "There’s a lot more for us to do. We have a few weeks left in the lame duck [session] and, frankly, a few big, big issues ahead. I want to see us do as much as we possibly can while we still have this majority," Scalise said. "I’ve got a lot more gas in the tank. Obviously, all of us know there’s some real change coming in January. We still have work to do right now." Jordan beat out Scalise in a 106-73 vote in Tuesday’s GOP elections. Scalise, who was elected in 2008 and first joined Republican leadership in 2014, proved a steady figure and mouthpiece for conservative principles even as the party shifted dramatically around him. Scalise originally served as House whip alongside Speaker John Boehner, R-Ohio. JORDAN EMERGES AS POTENTIAL NEXT GOP LEADER IF DEMS SEIZE HOUSE Although Boehner would eventually step down after the right flank of the party accused him of failing to secure GOP priorities, Scalise remained a constant, continuing to serve as whip under his successor, Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis. Around the same time, Donald Trump, then just a candidate for president, began gaining momentum in the GOP primary. As the party’s core began to gravitate toward Trump, Scalise’s time in Congress and personal well-being were challenged when he was shot at a congressional baseball practice in 2017. Although the incident left him with health complications, the attack elevated Scalise’s national profile. "Just left hospital. Rep. Steve Scalise, one of the truly great people, is in very tough shape — but he is a real fighter. Pray for Steve!" Trump said in a post to social media at the time. In 2023, Scalise would climb to the No. 2 job, becoming majority leader after Republicans recaptured the House of Representatives under Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif. And when McCarthy himself was removed from the post for failing to deliver Republican demands to cut spending, Scalise launched an unsuccessful bid for speaker. Instead, Scalise remained majority leader as Republicans rallied around Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. Asked if he would have done anything differently in his most recent bid to lead the House GOP, Scalise said he had no regrets. "Nothing that could have been done differently in the leadership race," Scalise said. MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS "There’s clearly a lot of weight lifted now. I mean, these leadership jobs take a lot of time, a lot of focus. I love doing the work… it takes you away from your family, from other things that you enjoy doing back home. I’ll have a little more free time there," he added. Following the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Republicans have a little under seven weeks to press for legislative priorities with their majorities in the House and Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The 120th Congress is set to begin on Jan. 3, 2027.

articles.title: Trump's ex-lawyer Alina Habba loses massive contract days after president blasts 'outrageous' deal
articles.summary: Donald Trump personally directed Alina Habba's firing from a $50 million Concord Partners contract linked to pardoned Venezuelan banker's family.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's former personal attorney, Alina Habba Mildon, has lost a four-year contract worth more than $50 million to serve as general counsel for a company founded by the daughter of a Venezuelan billionaire Trump pardoned earlier this year, according to The New York Times. Concord Partners, a Florida-based company founded by Isabela Herrera, daughter of Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini, terminated Habba Mildon’s contract after President Donald Trump urged the Herrera family to stop paying her, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported Wednesday. A source familiar with the matter confirmed the termination to Fox News Digital. TRUMP SIGNS PARDONS FOR ALASKA DIESEL MECHANICS ONSTAGE DURING RALLY TOUTING MAJOR ENERGY DEALS Concord Partners cited a "failure to perform duties" in a Nov. 4 termination letter obtained by The New York Times. Trump pardoned Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini Jan. 15, 2026, just two weeks after Habba Mildon began working for the company founded by his daughter. Herrera faced federal bribery charges tied to an alleged scheme involving Puerto Rico’s governor and struck a plea deal accepting a misdemeanor campaign finance violation in August 2025. The firing came just days after Trump publicly blasted Habba Mildon’s $50 million arrangement as excessive and said he did not want her to receive the money. "I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Mar-a-Lago Oct. 31, Reuters reported. "I told her, and I said, 'I don't want her paid.'" He called the arrangement "totally obnoxious and outrageous" and "not acceptable." Habba Mildon has denied playing any role in securing Herrera Velutini's pardon, pushing back against questions about whether her contract was connected to the president's decision. DOJ OPENS INVESTIGATION INTO TRUMP ALLY COREY LEWANDOWSKI "The Fake News still seems very confused by this so let me be even more clear: I was never paid to secure a pardon. I never met with anyone at the White House or DOJ about a pardon. I’ve never done any work in any capacity whatsoever for a pardon for anyone, period," Habba Mildon wrote on X Oct. 21. Habba Mildon signed the agreement with Concord Partners in October 2025 while serving as acting U.S. attorney for New Jersey. She began working for the company on Jan. 1, 2026, after becoming a senior advisor to Attorney General Pam Bondi, according to the outlet. Habba Mildon had already received about $14.5 million, including an $8 million signing bonus and $6.5 million in additional payments, according to The New York Times. MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Habba Mildon and the White House for comment.

articles.title: Democrats lambast absent peers after Republicans block Hegseth impeachment attempt
articles.summary: Eleven Democrats missed the key procedural vote on the impeachment effort, which failed by just seven votes
articles.body:
Democratic lawmakers expressed outrage at nearly a dozen of their colleagues for missing a vote Tuesday evening to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , allowing Republicans to defeat the effort.

Eleven Democrats missed the key procedural vote on the impeachment effort , which failed by just seven votes. Some blamed traffic and conflicting events and others accused Speaker Mike Johnson of closing the vote early. Many of those not in the Capitol said they support the effort to impeach Hegseth.

"You should show up and do your job," Abdul El-Sayed , the senator-elect of Michigan, said on CNN to the Democratic lawmakers Tuesday.

Richard Ojeda, the representative-elect of North Carolina, told CNN that the Democratic representatives "failed" by not voting.

"Shame on them for not showing up," Ojeda said on Tuesday. "I mean, this is important … they had an opportunity to finally get rid of this buffoonery we had."

The missing Democrats gave House Republicans the numbers to shelve the impeachment effort by voting 211 – 204 to refer eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a House committee.

Speaking at Arlington national cemetery to mark Veterans Day, Donald Trump praised Hegseth and said he had done a "fantastic job" as the Pentagon head.

"I had a feeling that was going to happen," the president said of the failed effort to impeach Hegseth, adding: "He loves you, and he protects you – he's all about you."

The articles, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie , included charges of violating congressional authority by waging war in Iran . The effort came after voters overwhelming cast ballots for Democratic candidates in the 2026 midterms, largely in rebuke of the Trump administration's policies – including the war in Iran.

Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a representative from California, told MeidasTouch there was "no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues".

"This is what the people have been talking about … so shame on folks who were not here because these people lost," Kamlager-Dove added.

Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico wrote on X that she was "blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due to a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote".

"When she reached the chamber the vote had just gaveled out. She immediately filed a report of her vote of 'NO' to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record," Stansbury wrote, adding that Hegseth "must be impeached now".

Laura Gillen of New York similarly wrote on X she too was stuck in traffic but "strongly" believes Hegseth should be impeached. Jonathan Jackson, of Illinois, wrote on X that he also was stuck behind the traffic jam.

Brittany Pettersen of Colorado wrote on X that she was "denied" the ability to vote. Member of Pettersen's office later told 9News she too was stuck in traffic.

Julia Brownley of California wrote on Facebook that Johnson "closed the vote" before she could make it to the House floor.

"As I and many of my colleagues were rushing to the floor to support Hegseth's impeachment, Mike Johnson closed the vote before we could," Brownley wrote.

Marilyn Strickland of Washington also missed the vote by one minute because she was stuck behind a motocade, but that she would have voted to impeach Hegseth, Strickland's office told Politico .

Nancy Pelosi of California missed the vote because she was in San Francisco to meet with local veterans and accept a Lifetime Advocate for Veterans Award, Pelosi's spokesperson told SFGate .

Lou Correa of California wrote on Instagram that he was undergoing a medical procedure and remaining in his district until he was medically cleared.

Steven Horsford of Nevada, Haley Stevens of Michigan and Frederica Wilson of Florida did not provide public reasons for their absence on Tuesday.

Several Democratic lawmakers who did vote on the effort to impeach Hegseth noted that they were also busy with other life events but still made their way to the Capitol.

Pat Ryan of New York wrote on X that he was recovering from back surgery but left the hospital early in order to cast his vote.

Congressman Glenn Ivey, a Maryland Democrat, called the absence of the 11 lawmakers during Tuesday's vote "certainly disappointing", but said there would be "other chances" to advance impeachment efforts.

In an interview, Ivey said he was "absolutely" supportive of renewing the push when Democrats regain control of both chambers in January.

At the same time, he argued that voters made clear that concerns about the cost of living remain their top priority.

"There aren't a lot of people, in my district anyway, [whose ability] to stay in their house depends on whether Hegseth gets impeached or not," Ivey said. "We've been calling it the affordability agenda, but I think for many people, it's really a survivability agenda, and we need to be focused on that."

• This story was updated on 11 November 2026. A previous version incorrectly stated that Brittany Pettersen is a lawmaker from California; she is from Colorado.

articles.title: Miller’s moment: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, we explore how Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff is already making waves across Washington.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we explore how Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff is already making waves across Washington. Plus, Andrea Mitchell digs into the alleged spy scandal that’s ensnared a top tech CEO. — Adam Wollner Democrats are deeply skeptical Trump wants to work with them after Stephen Miller’s elevation By Peter Nicholas After the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump said he’s open to cutting a deal with Democrats on immigration and showing he can work cooperatively with the opposition. But what Trump actually did was far more illustrative of what’s to come, as Democrats see it. Trump ousted Susie Wiles and installed as his new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, the face of hard-line immigration enforcement and an operative who has swung a rhetorical cleaver at the party that will soon control Congress. Miller won’t get a honeymoon from ascendant Democratic lawmakers whose party he likened last year to a “domestic extremist organization.” He’d need to shed the persona of an uncompromising Trump loyalist, and the early signs suggest he won’t, Democratic lawmakers told NBC News. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become House speaker when the new Congress convenes in January, called Miller a “stone-cold racist” in remarks to reporters Monday. Jeffries said he has “zero interest” in working with Miller. A reporter asked if Miller can be a viable partner to Democrats. “No,” Jeffries said. “Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. His track record speaks for itself. And I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.” To that end: The country’s top 16 Latino advocacy organizations are calling on the next Congress to subpoena Miller to answer for Trump’s mass deportation actions, Natasha Korecki reports. They’re also asking Congress to freeze any new funding for ICE until there is transparency in how money has already been spent. Friends in high places: Meanwhile, advocates of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement are enthusiastically embracing Miller as a new champion of their agenda in the White House, Aria Bendix writes. The group, which had been vocal about its disappointment with the Trump administration before the midterms, cheered Wiles’ exit. Read more → The alleged spy scandal shaking Washington and Silicon Valley Analysis by Andrea Mitchell It’s a Washington scandal that has the plot lines of pulp fiction: an alleged Chinese spy, exposed in a suspected romantic relationship with one of the world’s richest and most influential tech giants. As the president of the United States expresses sympathy for his friend and business ally, rather than disappointment or condemnation, questions persist about who knew what and when. The context is potentially even more damaging. Last year, Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio wrote a classified memo warning that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might be compromised by his friendship with a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times, citing multiple people briefed on the matter. The Times also reported that Rubio repeated that warning in May, en route to a Beijing summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Nevertheless, Huang was added to the corporate delegation traveling with President Donald Trump when Air Force One stopped to refuel in Alaska. He was also literally seated at the president’s right hand when Xi visited the White House last month. Asked Monday if he’d read Rubio’s memo when he brought Huang to Beijing, Trump said, “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Trump also said during the same exchange: “No, I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had, he — I asked him today because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right. … I asked him that question. ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him.” There have apparently been U.S. suspicions about Huang’s alleged romantic partner, Alice Huang (no relation), for a while. A former Chinese state media reporter, she purchased a subsidiary of a Chinese video gaming company that she turned into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based technology company. The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed at least a year ago over alleged backdoor shipments of Nvidia’s most prized advanced chips to Beijing — chips that the U.S. bans for sale to China under export controls. Nvidia’s most powerful chips dominate the market for data centers that are essential for artificial intelligence in the U.S. and Southeast Asia. In addition to his company being a top donor to the White House ballroom, according to documents obtained by The Washington Post, Huang has become a key adviser to Trump on major AI policy decisions. This year, Huang led a successful campaign to push back against government regulation of AI, instead arguing for the industry to adopt voluntary practices to keep new models safe. China has denounced the espionage allegations as a smear. Jensen Huang acknowledged being “unfaithful” to his wife over the weekend, but did not mention Alice Huang. Rubio has declined to comment on the scandal, nor has the White House explained Trump’s Monday statements that he did not recall being warned. Nvidia is investigating but asserted it does not believe any corporate or U.S. secrets were compromised. The company’s stock has also taken a hit this week. Huang has no known succession plan in place in case action is taken to remove him from his hugely profitable company, with fears this scandal could even affect the U.S. economy, which has been heavily dependent on the AI boom. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race, breaking the GOP’s grip on the state
articles.summary: Colom pulled off an upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Mississippi since 1982.
articles.body: In a major upset, Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, NBC News projects, capping off a string of Democratic victories by flipping the reddest seat yet in this year’s midterms. Mississippi last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago, just a few weeks before Colom was born in 1982. Colom will become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The historic win comes after days of uncertainty in the race, with Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith as more votes continued to be counted. Colom, a district attorney, remained confident throughout the vote counting that he would prevail. Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video message Wednesday evening. “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.” Colom is expected to address his supporters at a victory party later Wednesday night. Colom’s campaign confirmed to NBC News that Hyde-Smith had called him to concede. Colom’s victory means Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats next year. The only Senate race left to be called is in Alaska. In the next Congress, no Democratic senator will represent a redder state than Colom. Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024. Colom’s victory also underscores the Trump administration’s broad unpopularity with voters just two years after that presidential election, even in parts of the ruby-red Deep South. A majority of Mississippi voters said they disapproved of Trump’s overall job performance, according to NBC News exit polling. Majorities also said that his policies, including tariffs, hurt the economy and that it was wrong for the U.S. to take military action in Iran. Colom, the eighth Democrat to flip a Republican-held Senate seat so far this year, long believed Democrats had an opportunity to win Mississippi, given its sizable Black population and plenty of white voters in rural areas who he thought could back a Democrat. He chided his party for writing off the state. “We were never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause,” Colom recently told NBC News. “We were betrayed by Cindy Hyde-Smith because she allowed tariffs to hurt us. She allowed people — hundreds of thousands of Mississippians — to lose healthcare. She gave away our voice in the war in Iran, which drove up costs for farmers and for truckers and for businesses.” “But for too long we were also a betrayed cause by the national party, because they did not compete in this state,” Colom added. In late October, the Senate Majority PAC, a top Democratic super PAC, announced an ad campaign in the state through Election Day, starting with a 30-second spot that presented Colom as a crusader who would “fight corruption in both parties.” The group ended up spending nearly $2.1 million on the airwaves, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. The GOP super PAC Senate Leadership Fund responded with a similar-sized buy, airing ads that painted Colom as “too liberal” and “too radical.” The race also drew high-profile surrogates from both parties. Trump traveled to Mississippi eight days before the election, while Democrats such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia hit the campaign trail for Colom. Former President Barack Obama also appeared in an ad that the Colom campaign launched on digital platforms. Republicans tried to leverage those surrogates against Colom, with the Senate Leadership Fund launching one ad with a narrator saying, “Colom proudly campaigns with Kamala Harris because Colom supports their radical agenda.” But it was not enough to defeat Colom, who sharply criticized Hyde-Smith’s vote for Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which cut Medicaid funds. Colom also faulted Hyde-Smith’s support for the Trump administration’s tariff regime and the costly war with Iran, labeling his opponent “Cindy High Prices.” Colom’s campaign also created a viral video highlighting Hyde-Smith’s comments that Mississippians struggling with high beef prices “have so many proteins to choose from.” The video featured clips of people saying: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator.” Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner who was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and won a full term in 2020, campaigned as a reliable conservative and tried to portray Colom as a “radical” progressive. She also touted her loyalty to Trump, who endorsed her more than a year before the midterms and said she was “100% MAGA.” Hyde-Smith said that over the last week, her campaign team “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.” “I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: An election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will,” she said. Colom and Hyde-Smith had crossed paths before this year’s midterm elections. She blocked his nomination for a federal judgeship during the Biden administration. Colom recently told NBC News that he had forgiven her.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom seals historic win in Mississippi Senate race
articles.summary: Colom is the first black person from the southern state elected to the US Senate in over 140 years.
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.

Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.

Only a few thousand votes separated Colom from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The margin was so close that the race could not be called until more than a week after election day, as local officials counted every single ballot that had arrived before the deadline.

Colon won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.

Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.

"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.

The result means the Democratic majority in the Senate is now 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.

It also wipes away a Republican winning streak in Mississippi that dates back to 1982.

The Mississippi contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.

But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections as the party won control of both the House and the Senate.

It has won Senate seats in numerous Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.

Colom appeared to a ride a national wave of resentment against Republicans, with the party suffering several defeats during the midterm election in typically conservative strongholds like Texas, Kansas and Iowa.

Voter backlash against Trump's Republican party has been driven in large part by economic woes, blamed on his administration's tariffs and war with Iran, according to exit polls.

Colom, a local prosecutor, used the national mood to his advantage, highlighting his opponent's support for Trump's tariffs and giving her the nickname "Cindy High Prices".

The Democrat campaigned aggressively, visiting all of Mississippi's 82 counties.

Hyde-Smith's campaign assailed Colom as a puppet of billionaire liberal donor George Soros, whose family has helped fund the Democrat's political campaigns.

The Republican was criticised for a lack of public appearances.

articles.title: Army sentinel sharply reprimands Hegseth's group at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day

articles.body: An Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery called for silence and respect Wednesday after laughter was heard from departing members of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's entourage following a Veterans Day ceremony. Video shows the incident unfolding shortly after President Donald Trump left the memorial following a wreath-laying ceremony. Trump left the memorial around 12:28 p.m. Hegseth and members of his entourage, including his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, began taking photos and posing on the memorial steps around 12:29 p.m., according to the video. TRUMP UNLOADS ON AOC, MAMDANI FOR LAUGHING DURING SACRED 9/11 CEREMONY AT GROUND ZERO Roughly a minute later, laughter could be heard in the distance as members of the group departed, prompting a soldier guarding the tomb to issue a sharp reminder to those gathered. "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times," the soldier said. The instruction came around 12:30 p.m., after Trump had left the ceremony. TRAVELERS UNITE IN POWERFUL MOMENT OF SILENCE AS FALLEN US SERVICE MEMBER RETURNS HOME Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell responded to the incident in a statement to Fox News, emphasizing the department's commitment to honoring fallen service members. "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," Parnell said. "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum." The soldiers who guard the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier are known as sentinels and belong to the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, also known as The Old Guard. articles.title: Dems projected to score historic upset in deep-red Mississippi, topple Trump ally Hyde-Smith
articles.summary: U.S. Senate Republicans suffered another stunning setback as Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is projected to lose to Democrat Scott Colom in reliably red Mississippi, according to the AP.
articles.body: Senate Republicans are projected to suffer yet another stunning setback, this time in reliably red Mississippi. Incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., is projected to lose her bid for a second full term in the U.S. Senate to state District Attorney Scott Colom in a race that was deadlocked until the final weeks of October, according to The Associated Press. More than a week after Election Day, the AP called the razor-thin race in favor of Colom Wednesday, pushing the Democrats' hold on the U.S. Senate to 55 seats to the Republicans' 44 in another flip. SOROS NETWORK TARGETS DEEP-RED MISSISSIPPI IN BID TO FLIP SENATE SEAT Democrats could gain another pending the results in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola is in a neck-and-neck contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. A source told Fox News Digital Hyde-Smith had spoken with Colom and conceded the race. Colom's victory over Hyde-Smith marked a historic moment in the Magnolia State, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since the 1980s. Hyde-Smith, in a video posted to X, said, "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state." His win comes after President Donald Trump rallied behind Hyde-Smith and a seven-figure, last-minute ad buy by the Senate Leadership Fund, a political action committee closely tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., was not enough to stop Colom’s momentum. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., took a victory lap before the race was officially called by The Associated Press, congratulating Colom on his historic win in a state that once seemed unattainable. "Congratulations to Senator-Elect Colom on his historic win and on becoming the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat in over four decades," the lawmakers said. "We will work hand in hand with Scott to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs and future in the 120th Congress and look forward to welcoming him to our caucus." Hyde-Smith's loss to Colom, who she previously blocked for a district court seat under the Biden administration years ago, comes after both parties rallied big names and resources in an effort to prevent a nightmare scenario for Republicans.But in a previous interview with Fox News Digital, Colom said that wasn't his motivating factor. "I mean, as a district attorney, I have to prosecute cases where people lost their loved ones to gun violence. So, you know, and I’ve seen them forgive that person. "So, that's not the motivating factor," he continued. "For me, it's really the betrayal of the America First movement, right? Like she was supposed to help President Trump get lower grocery prices. Well, she betrayed us. We're not getting lower grocery prices."

articles.title: Mississippi Senate results: Scott Colom narrowly defeats Cindy Hyde-Smith, flipping another seat for Democrats in midterm elections
articles.summary: The outcome, after a prolonged ballot-counting process, signifies a major shift in Mississippi, which has been staunchly Republican for decades.
articles.body:
Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday to flip another Senate seat for Democrats.

According to figures from the Associated Press, Colom won 49.2% of the vote in the closely contested race that was called more than a week after Election Day. Hyde-Smith finished with 48.7%.

Mississippi — one of the reddest states in the country — wasn't really on the national radar prior to the elections. However, early results showed the two candidates separated by as few as 43 votes, indicating a shock was brewing.

The outcome expands Democrats' total number of Senate seats to 55, giving the party its largest midterm gain since 1986 — a rout that has seen the GOP lose control of the Senate and House.

Colom becomes the first elected Black U.S. senator from Mississippi in more than 140 years and the state's first Democratic senator since 1989.

Prior to the result being declared, Colom had repeatedly expressed confidence that his campaign would prevail, flooding the airwaves and attending at least eight events. "It's very clear the direction of this," he told reporters on Friday .

Hyde-Smith delivered a concession message in a video posted on X Wednesday evening : "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

Alaska is now the only remaining Senate race to be called. Democrat Mary Peltola holds the lead on 49%, with 84% of the vote counted. Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan is on 47.2%, according to the latest AP figures.

Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus.

In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases.

In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination.

"I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times .

But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ."

In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper."

Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy.

Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since.

There were signs before Election Day that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%.

Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn.

Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from."

In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 19 million views on Colom's X account .

When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom.

In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own).

In the end, it wasn't enough to secure Hyde-Smith victory. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom went to his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices.

"I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for."

articles.title: At least 9 new Dem members will carry Al Green's mantle and try to impeach President Trump
articles.summary: Rep. Al Green says at least nine incoming House Democratic caucus members will join his impeachment push, citing President Trump's crypto dealings and what they described as corruption.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: At least 9 incoming progressive members of the House Democratic caucus are expected to support efforts to impeach President Donald Trump, continuing a push led by outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, Fox News Digital has learned. Green and representatives from the Removal Coalition and Courage for Democracy Project discussed the effort with Fox News Digital after a Capitol Hill news conference, months after the Texas Democrat introduced articles of impeachment against Trump in August. Green is counting on support from Reps.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo.; Dan Koh, D-Mass.; Chris Rabb, D-Pa.; Angela Gonzales-Torres, D-Calif.; and several other incoming Democrats to continue his impeachment efforts after he leaves Congress. DEMOCRAT AL GREEN TO FORCE HOUSE-WIDE VOTE ON IMPEACHING TRUMP "Impeachment is the only means for our future. We cannot deal with a president who engages in corruption," Green told Fox News Digital. "The end is to have the president removed from office. I applaud the courageous members carrying these efforts into the next Congress." Green pointed to Trump's cryptocurrency dealings as one example of what he characterized as corruption by the president. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE Gonzales-Torres told Fox News Digital she intends to continue Green's efforts while representing the more than 100,000 Los Angeles voters she said elected her to Congress. The coalition acknowledged uncertainty over whether its impeachment efforts would succeed, noting that even if the House approved articles against Trump, the Senate could again decline to convict him, as it did in Trump’s two previous impeachment trials. TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS However, organizers expressed confidence that growing grassroots pressure could persuade additional Democratic lawmakers to support impeachment. "The more we articulate this effort and talk about why it is so crucial that we get rid of Trump, the more support we will have," Keira Havens, co-founder of the Courage for Democracy Project, told Fox News Digital. Havens acknowledged that some Democrats who oppose Trump may still reject impeachment articles because they believe the allegations lack sufficient legal grounds or that conviction would fail in the Senate. A constitutional expert affiliated with the Courage for Democracy Project also argued that Senate impeachment procedures could provide additional avenues for removing a president, citing Rule VIII. However, the Constitution gives the House the sole power of impeachment and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments. PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP Jessica Denson, identified as the founder of the Removal Coalition, criticized Democratic lawmakers who have prioritized congressional hearings and potential prosecutions of Trump administration officials over impeaching the president himself. Denson called those lawmakers "spineless," arguing that grassroots pressure could eventually push them to support the coalition's demands. The coalition told Fox News Digital that "hearings and prosecutions aren't enough," and enough public backlash will lead any remaining Democratic lawmaker to get behind impeachment efforts. The effort comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, potentially giving impeachment supporters a greater opportunity to advance resolutions against Trump. Under the Constitution, impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, while conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority of senators present. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP During and after the news conference, the coalition, consisting of the two advocacy organizations and incoming and outgoing lawmakers, told Fox News Digital it also intends to pursue impeachment proceedings against War Secretary Pete Hegseth. The coalition argued that Hegseth should face impeachment alongside Trump, claiming that any wrongdoing uncovered involving the war secretary could also implicate the president. However, a finding of wrongdoing by Hegseth would not automatically establish legal or constitutional liability for Trump. Trump and Hegseth did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Peanut the squirrel’s former owner has been detained by ICE, could be deported
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security under President Donald Trump has put one of the late squirrel’s owners in an immigration jail, pending possible deportation to Germany.
articles.body: PINE CITY, N.Y. — When New York wildlife officers euthanized a couple’s pet squirrel, Peanut, two years ago, Republicans including JD Vance seized on the critter’s killing as just another example of government overreach from meddling Democrats. “The same government that doesn’t care about hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrant criminals coming into our country doesn’t want us to have pets. It’s the craziest, the craziest thing,” Vance said at a rally just before the 2024 election. Now, the Department of Homeland Security under President Donald Trump has put one of the late squirrel’s owners in an immigration jail, pending possible deportation to Germany. Daniela Bittner was arrested by immigration officers in mid-October at a small airport near New York’s border with Pennsylvania. DHS issued a statement saying Bittner was arrested because she “chose to overstay her welcome in defiance of our nation’s laws.” Since then, Bittner has been moved through multiple immigration lockups and is now housed in Texas, according to her husband, Mark Longo, who called conditions in the lockups “deplorable.” He blamed her detention on an immigration paperwork mix-up. “They put Peanut on a pedestal, won their election, and threw him off that pedestal immediately,” Longo said. The arrest was the latest twist in the tale of Peanut, also known as P’nut, a once-orphaned squirrel whose fun antics made him a social media star. That is, until state officials got multiple complaints that the couple were illegally keeping wild animals in their house as pets, including the squirrel and a racoon. During one inspection, Peanut bit the gloved thumb of a wildlife biologist and was euthanized so the squirrel could be tested for rabies. News stories about the episode earned the family sympathy and caught the attention of Republicans on the campaign trail, who criticized the state’s response and New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul. Longo said he tries to steer clear of politics, but that he can’t help but feel like the government keeps wading into his life. “I’m begging the world to find an answer as to why this keeps happening to me,” he told The Associated Press by phone Wednesday. “One time, you can call it what it is. Two times, it’s now becoming a little bit more of a target.” Longo said he and Bittner made a mistake on one of her immigration forms and didn’t catch the error while they were dealing with the dustup over Peanut’s seizure and killing. “You know, arrest the people who deserve to be arrested. My wife is not one of them,” he said. “You’re telling me, all of this because my wife and I forgot to do the proper form?” he added. Longo said local officials have been looking into his wife’s case and that he’s spoken about her arrest to UFC chief Dana White, a longstanding ally of President Donald Trump whom Longo said he met after Peanut was taken. Longo said he will have to shut down the animal sanctuary he and his wife run if she is deported. “The only outcome that will save this place is my wife not being deported,” he said.

articles.title: Cameroon: Who is really calling the shots?
articles.summary: Biya’s absences raise questions about who holds power and what comes next in Cameroon.
articles.body:
Yaounde, Cameroon – A dispute over roadworks in Yaounde in March, ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Cameroon the following month, highlighted tensions between central government and municipal authorities.

The disagreement involved Housing and Urban Development Minister Celestine Ketcha Courtes and Yaounde City Mayor Luc Messi Atangana over the rehabilitation of a road along the papal visit route, according to local media reports.

The episode raised a broader question about competing centres of authority in Cameroon: Who exercises power when President Paul Biya is absent?

Biya, 93, has governed Cameroon since 1982. His prolonged absences from public view have intensified scrutiny on how decisions are made, who has access to him and how much authority is exercised by those around him.

Biya returned to Yaounde on August 20 after more than 10 weeks abroad, following a stay in Europe that began on June 7 . His return did little to dispel questions about the management of power.

The issue is not simply whether the state continues to function. It is whether the institutions and informal networks built around one president can manage power coherently when he is not visibly directing government.

Cameroon’s constitution gives the president extensive executive authority. He defines national policy, appoints the prime minister and, based on the latter’s proposal, other members of government.

He is also commander-in-chief of the armed forces. The prime minister heads the government and directs its activities within the framework of the president’s policy.

Under Section 10 of the constitution, the president may delegate some of his powers to the prime minister, other members of government and senior administrative officials, within the scope of their respective responsibilities.

Where the president is temporarily unable to perform his duties, he must expressly delegate some of his functions to the prime minister or, if the prime minister is also unavailable, another member of government.

An absence abroad does not, in itself, establish that the president is temporarily unable to perform his duties or automatically transfer his constitutional powers to the prime minister.

The government has not provided a detailed public account of whether a clear delegation of presidential functions is in effect during Biya’s prolonged absences.

Research by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) found that Biya spent at least four and a half years abroad on private visits over a period of more than three decades.

The investigation, which examined records of his travels from 1982 onwards, renewed questions about how much government business depends on his direct involvement.

One figure central to that debate is Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh, the secretary-general at the presidency.

According to the official biography published by the Prime Minister’s Office, his responsibilities include receiving the president’s instructions, monitoring the implementation of presidential decisions and coordinating administrations attached to the presidency.

On February 5, 2019, Biya signed Decree No. 2019/043, granting Ngoh Ngoh a permanent delegation of signature. The measure gave him authority to sign certain official documents on the president’s behalf.

A delegation of signature, however, is not a transfer of presidential powers. Ngoh Ngoh is not constitutionally the president’s successor, and his formal responsibilities should not be confused with the informal political influence attributed to him.

Other figures regularly mentioned in discussions about the presidency include First Lady Chantal Biya and the president’s son, Franck Biya. Neither holds a constitutional executive office. Claims about their influence and about rival networks around the president are difficult to establish independently.

Ryan Cummings, an Africa-focused security analyst, has argued that individuals close to the president may be playing increasingly tangible roles as questions grow about the management of power.

His assessment points to the importance of the presidential circle but does not establish who makes particular decisions or on whose authority.

Access to the president does not, in itself, establish that those around him exercise executive powers.

The succession question has become more pressing following a constitutional amendment approved on April 14 this year. The amendment reintroduced the office of vice president, with the president given the authority to appoint and dismiss its holder.

Under the revised Article 6, the vice president would assume the presidency if the office became vacant through the president’s death, resignation or permanent incapacity established by the Constitutional Council.

The vice president would complete the remainder of the presidential term.

The law also provides for circumstances in which there is no vice president or the vice president is unable to perform the duties of the office. In either case, a presidential election must be held between 20 and 120 days after the post officially becomes vacant.

The Senate president would serve as interim president until a new president is elected. If the Senate president is unable to perform the role, the responsibility passes to the Senate vice president, according to the order of precedence in the Senate.

The amendment establishes a formal succession mechanism but leaves the appointment of the vice president in Biya’s hands. As of November 10 , no appointment had been publicly announced.

The absence of a designated vice president means the new succession arrangement has yet to be tested. If the presidency became vacant before an appointment, the constitution provides for an interim presidency under the Senate president and a new presidential election. Accounts of competing factions and efforts to position potential successors should therefore be treated as assessments, not evidence of an agreed succession plan.

Military appointments during Biya’s absence have added another dimension to the debate.

On August 4 , the Reuters news agency reported that three presidential decrees had reshuffled the senior military leadership. The changes included replacing commanders in four of Cameroon’s five joint military regions, promoting the head of the Presidential Guard from colonel to brigadier general and appointing a new commander of the Rapid Intervention Brigade.

Robert Besseling, CEO of intelligence advisory firm Pangea-Risk, interprets the changes partly through the lens of loyalty and the management of potential threats to the presidency. The decrees do not explain the reasons for the appointments, making their political significance difficult to establish independently.

The stakes extend beyond the presidential palace. Cameroon faces a separatist conflict in its English-speaking regions and attacks by armed groups linked to Boko Haram in the Far North.

Uncertainty over political authority at the centre could complicate the government’s response to these challenges, even as state institutions continue to operate.

Opposition criticism has focused on the concentration of executive authority. Social Democratic Front leader Joshua Osih criticised the constitutional amendment during the parliamentary debate in April. In remarks reported by Focus Media Afrique on April 3 , he argued that the reform weakened democratic legitimacy and reinforced the centralisation of power.

The government, meanwhile, has defended the president’s authority to make appointments. Communication Minister and government spokesman Rene Emmanuel Sadi told French broadcaster RFI in August that Biya was entitled to decide when to form a new government. The presidency did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Not all observers see an immediate breakdown in state administration. Paul Anchang, a Yaounde-based political analyst, argues that institutions continue to perform their functions. Besseling, however, offers a more critical assessment of the political situation.

The distinction between a functioning state and an accountable centre of political authority remains at the heart of Cameroon’s predicament.

Government business may continue, but the concentration of power around one individual leaves unresolved questions about who exercises authority in his absence and how it will eventually be transferred.

As Robert Besseling puts it: “The political scene suffers from distinct institutional paralysis.”
